title: Missing break in a switch
summary: How a switch jumps to a case and keeps going, and three ways to make it stop where you mean.
objectives: Describe how a switch statement jumps to a case and then runs downwards.
Predict the output of a switch with missing `break` statements.
Use `break`, grouped cases and the arrow form correctly.
Recognise when falling through is deliberate.

blocks.text: A switch picks one case to run based on a value. Without `break`, it does not stop at the end of that case: it carries on into every case below it. Java calls this falling through.

bad.title: Falls through

good.title: Stops after its case

blocks.note: The day is 2, so only Tuesday should print. Without `break`, the switch prints three lines.

blocks.text: A case label is not a box around some code. It is a place to jump to. The switch finds the label that matches, jumps there, and then runs line after line, straight past the next labels, until it reaches a `break` or the end of the switch.

blocks.caption: switch (day) with day = 2 and no break
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([switch on day, which is 2]) --> B[Jump to case 2]
  B --> C[Print Tuesday]
  C --> D{break here?}
  D -- yes --> X([Leave the switch])
  D -- no --> E[Fall into case 3: print Wednesday]
  E --> F[Fall into default: print Another day]
  F --> X

blocks.caption: Tracing the version without break, day = 2

blocks.text: Without any `break`, the earlier the matching case, the more lines run. With a `break` after every case, each value prints exactly one line.

blocks.caption: Lines printed by the switch above, for each value of day

sections.title: When falling through is on purpose

blocks.text: Falling through is not always a mistake. Putting several labels on top of each other lets them share one body, which is the one common use of it.

blocks.title: Two labels, one body
Say so when you mean it
blocks.text: If a case really should continue into the next one after doing some work, write a comment such as `// falls through` on that line. Readers, and tools like Code Coach, then know it is deliberate.

sections.title: The modern fix: the arrow switch

blocks.text: Since Java 14 a switch can use `->` instead of a colon. An arrow case runs only its own code and never falls through, so there is no `break` to forget. Several values can share one arrow, separated by commas.

blocks.title: No break needed

bad.title: One break missing: pass becomes F

good.title: Each case stops

blocks.note: Only one `break` is missing, and the effect is quiet: the value is set and then immediately overwritten by the case below.

blocks.title: return also stops a case
blocks.text: Inside a method, `return` leaves the method and so leaves the switch too. A case that ends with `return` does not need a `break` after it.

blocks.question: day is 3 and the switch has no break statements. What prints?
blocks.explanation: The switch jumps to case 3, prints Wednesday, then falls into default and prints Another day.

blocks.question: Which statement stops a colon-style case from falling into the next one?
blocks.explanation: `break` leaves the switch. `continue` belongs to loops, and there is no brace around a case.

blocks.question: Which switch can never fall through?
options: One that switches on a String
blocks.explanation: Arrow cases run only their own code. The others can all fall through if a break is missing.

items: A case label is a jump target, not a fence: the switch runs on until break or the end.
Put `break` at the end of every colon-style case unless you mean it to fall through.
Stacking labels (`case 6: case 7:`) is the deliberate, common use of falling through.
The arrow form, `case 1 ->`, never falls through and needs no `break`.
A case that ends with `return` does not need a `break`.
